title: What would you rate your level of suspension of disbelief when watching movies?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

it really depends on how much the story sucks me in and how effective/magnetic the performances are. you can serve me any kind of nonsense and i'm in. (see all the craziness that Max & Furiosa get into as they go east and then turn around.)  
if i don't connect, then my brain will start asking questions...

I think I'm an outlier. I truly have no problem suspending my disbelief no matter how ridiculous the premise is. Whatever rules you setup I'm there for. The only times I start having my immersion broken is if (1) the movie's internal logic starts to be inconsistent. A recent example for me was *No One Will Save You* where it started to not make sense why she wouldn't make any noise. Or (2) the film starts to overexplain things so that it forces me to question everything. For me that's the film *Yesterday* which I cannot stand because it starts to randomly show certain products that don't exist and yet all of modern music is the same even though a really important band was removed. Just stick with the setup and don't worry about the details in this instance because all it proves is that you didn't think about any of it.

If that's the spectrum, I'm not sure where I fit. I don't care if a movie is "realistic," but I do want it to make sense. That is, I want it to be consistent with its own premises, however wacky those premises may be. I'm fine with surreal movies as long as they're *supposed* to be surreal. E.g. *Mulholland Drive*. But I'm not fine with lazy movies that pretend to take place in the real world but can't be bothered getting details right. Can't think of a good example at the moment.

I'm also not fine with movies with fantastic premises if they fail to hold to those premises consistently. E.g. Total Recall (1990). If you want me to believe the action may be taking place in Quaid's head, don't show me extended scenes with action of which Quaid is completely unaware. That tells me that either a) The action *isn't* all in his head, or b) the film-makers are too stupid to be consistent, or c) they're too lazy and figure I'm an idiot who will just think the movie is kewl. Whichever option is correct, I've lost interest.

A big thing that affect my suspension of disbelief is how well the cuts between shots are handled. When it cuts to another angle and the actors' posture or facial expression is slightly different, it really takes me out of it because I can tell it's two different takes. 

I'm not sure whether this is controlled more by the actor, director, or editor, but some movies definitely have more bad cuts than others.

If I want to watch something for how “realistic” it is then I’d watch a documentary or the news.

I’m a lawyer and I enjoy legal movies despite being clearly incorrect on 99% of how the legal world works. It’s part of the fun. A fictional work giving people an incorrect perception about some real-world thing sucks and is unfortunate, but I don’t think it’s something worth caring much about

One -:being I want everything to feel airtight, logical, cohesive, characters to act as believably they can and ten being cars moving 500 ft in the air.


Actually think I would give myself a six.

Six is initially generous in terms of suspension of disbelief ..I'm not particularly judgmental on a plot not being perfect or a character acting in a way that isn't reflective of how real life individuals act.

A good example of this is the 2006 casino royale embassy sequence.

There's a part in the film where they show the security camera but also Bond seeming to notice it.

A).Maybe the reason he does not shoot out the cameras is because the sound might alert the local guards.

B). Maybe he's afraid that taking his line of fire away from the terrorist would cause him to lose the suspect.

,
C). He doesn't care. He's inside anyway so he probably doesn't think that there's anything that security cameras can show that doesn't give information that will already be there.

I mean M criticizes Bond for not shooting out the security cameras.

My point is what happens in that segment is more important than why it happens. 

And so when it becomes to a point where I'm actively trying to care about the plot even though it feels silly, I think that's an issue with the storytelling and the concept of the work of art. 

I'm still trying to think of a Jurassic world as a  movie where the sales pitch is that" children are bored by watching real dinosaurs interact.".

I think the “willing” aspect of it is the important part. I’m willing to suspend my disbelief if I am properly compensated. Being “properly compensated” is a very deep rabbit hole that I’m not going to go into, but if I feel like it’s worth it, I can suspend my disbelief pretty fucking far.

As some people have already said. it needs to make sense within its own established rules and world, whatever that world is. You can't go one way, and then suddenly go the other way. I was watching *The Changeling* last night (1980 horror movie with George C Scott) and i had no idea what the spirit wanted and what its actual powers was. One moment it was apparently stuck in a room, or another moment in a well, and the other moment it was picking up balls at the bottom of a river, or killing cops by turning their cars upside down. I really struggled to understand the internal consistency. Either you keep the spirit locked and get the main character to unlock it, or the spirit is omnipotent, it can't be both. So yeah, i'm probably a 9/10.

How dare you say that about total recall.  Also memory had been proven to be unreliable, to the point where people make up their own memories. This could include a memory of something happening that they were not privy to.

But that's well explained in the film, no? It's either cross a dried-up ocean for weeks, or go back for a chance to achieve something. Both are suicidal, but one choice can actually make a change. This makes sense in the set-up of the film's world. (Now, if we are talking about the crazy stunts, then that's another thing. Obviously they are crazy and unrealistic, but you are right, Miller sucks us in by clearly establishing that in this world, this is just Tuesday).

It isn't a matter of if can suspend my disbelief, but more of it everything they do fits into the reality they are creating. World rules matter. John Wick establishes that assassin's are everywhere but normal people mostly don't notice. If they suddenly started showing news programs talking about the murders it would be weird. 

As long as they follow their own world rules I can suspend disbelief 100% easy. The more and more they ignore their own rules or worse yet make up rules as they go along and then drop the rule when it isn't useful anymore then I get really really annoyed.

It's a film.

I know I'm watching a film.

How realistic should it be?  Depends on what the film is trying to do.

There's a moment in Atomic Blonde where protagonist states she had her bags sent.  Apparently, director did this to explain why she had no luggage even though she would have a ton of costume changes later.  I kinda appreciate that... but, honestly, when I saw the film I thought that information was being given to viewer because of some significance we'd be shown.  Feels like a Chekhov's gun.  As such, I don't want that dialogue included.  Realistic?  I guess it's more realistic... but I know it's a movie.  I'm not gonna forget it's a movie...

I think suspending your disbelief is a skill you have to work to cultivate. It requires you to be actively engaged with the film, regardless of its premise or accuracy. Nit picking and critiquing believablity happens after the movie is over, but during, i try to stay as engrossed as possible. Its not always possible, sometimes a moment will shatter my suspension, but i pride myself on my ability to take a film seriously even if it was never meant to be.

I just want consistency within the story. If the movie lets you know early on that shit is gonna get weird then I’m gonna let a lot of things slide. But if a movie tries to be super realistic I’m going to nitpick it a lot more

My big thing is I'm the most drawn to a movie that belongs to itself.  And what I mean by that is, a movie that's all-in, commits, creates it's own world, set of rules and the story and characters flow through it.

One could say that's all movies but that isn't necessarily so.  I do not like to be pandered to/begged for approval.  

I do not care what the premise is or how outlandish it is, if the movie belongs to itself and I'm lucky enough to peer into it, I can easily suspend disbelief--and also because, it's a movie.  It's fiction.  It's art.  It's all but not real outside of itself.

I don't really have an answer to you question, but I think it was Roger Ebert who said "audiences will sooner accept the impossible than the implausible," and I think that's sorta where I stand on this. I can buy all sorts of crazy shit as long as it's properly set up, but when characters act in a way that nobody would ever act — especially in the service of a plot point — that's when I start to get irked.

I've become very analytical when watching films, so I (21M) can enjoy them less now, which is ironic, because my love for the medium has grown over the past few years.

But there are films that are so capturing that defeat me and my unconscious need to act as a critic, and Immerse myself into the story.

The most recent one was Amadeus (1984).

The spirit was reliving what happened to him. He was trying to communicate with the main character any way he could. He didn’t have a power. He simply wanted the world to know he was murdered and replaced.

I love the genre of legal movies (IANAL), but I honestly don't know how you stand it. I work in academia and any time I see anything pertaining to faculty or research I wince so much, and just go full GEICO "that's not how any of this works!" I remember distinctly an episode of Grey's Anatomy where Derek Shepherd gets an article published in a journal and he and his research team are featured in a cover photo on the journal wearing scrubs. What? That doesn't happen, you don't have researchers on the cover like they're actually the sexiest people alive, what the hell is the matter with you?

But it also pivots me to one of my favorite movies featuring an academic, The Visitor, which seemed very grounded in its portrayal of a jaded academic, though it wasn't the main point of the movie. His speech about how he feels about his work doesn't matter much to him anymore is just such a great piece of writing.

Not a lawyer:

I can’t stand most any and all courtroom dramas, because of how unrealistic their legal manoeuvres seems. From my cousin Vinny to ‘you can’t handle the truth’, I always find Hollywood’s views about the the legal systems completely bogus. Even better representations seem fictitious.

True or false?

I think criticizing plot holes in a film (or any fiction really) is usually beside-the-point--the only times I'd say it really bothers me are when a work is clearly striving for some degree of realism but the lapses in "reality" are so jarring and frequent that it undercuts the tone, or when it's clearly symptomatic of a lack of effort put into the script.

I'm ready to believe whatever you throw at me, but tiny things bother me. Just watched Bloodshot with Vin Diesel, and in his 2nd big action sequence, it's announced that they collided with a flour truck, it's covered everything, looks like snow, and then they light flares without exploding.

If you can tell me a compelling story with consistent internal logic and consistent characterization, I’ll kick my disbelief straight into orbit. 

Some exceptions apply. I will notice and frown deeply if you: 

- do not account for comms delay in space. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, you can’t have a conversation in real time with Mission Control from your orbit around Jupiter. 
- people splitting up to be sneaky and then whispering to each other as if they have mics and earpieces when they don’t
- actually now that I’ve started to list them they are mostly about space. So I guess I’m like a 2 generally and a 7 or 8 for hard sci fi in space

>If you want me to believe the action may be taking place in Quaid's head, don't show me extended scenes with action of which Quaid is completely unaware.

This is what gets me about people who say the witches weren't real in The VVitch. Like you clearly see them in scenes independent of any character's subjectivity lol, how can they be anything but real.

I agree with what seems to be the common sentiment in the comments: as long as the movie sets up rules and sticks to those rules OR if it breaks those rules it needs to make sense in the story. 

Not that the MCU is high art but I often use this  example when asked why I don’t find those movies very interesting: a character is more engaging to watch when we know they have limits and their limits can be tested. I think Ironman is more fun to watch earlier on when his suits have problems that limit his abilities ie. their cumbersome, fuel reliant, limited weapons, they take damage… watching that character in a “nanotech” suit that sprawls from his chest and can cgi construct weapons and shields and repair itself is like if Die Hard but John McClane is invulnerable to harm.

The vast majority of what is depicted is not going to be realistic, both in and out of a courtroom. If that’s what you’re asking with “true or false”? 

But that’s for a good reason imo: the real job is, for the most part, incredibly slow and boring and repetitive. There’s a reason so many lawyers have alcohol/stress issues, and tell people to not become lawyers, because so many people end up hating it lol. A truly realistic legal show would bore everyone to tears, including other lawyers, because the moments of tension/excitement in a case are often only felt by knowing/experiencing a whole bunch of stuff prior to the actual impactful moment, if that makes sense. And you have to go through a ton of dull stuff to even get close to a moment like that.

My Cousin Vinny is actually one of the most accurate portrayals of a trial ever in a film: his cross of the state’s witnesses, as well as Mona Lisa’s expert testimony, is pretty much exactly how any lawyer would do all of that (minus the more dramatic/confrontational flare of everything of course), and whenever the judge would chew him out, it’d be for things any real judge would chew an atty out for doing

Anatomy of a Murder is also much more accurate than most

Legally Blonde is realistic about a decent amount of law school, including how the Harvard admins try to spin her Fashion major as a plus for “intellectual diversity” or whatever — law schools get a million Poli Sci/English major applicants, so they actually do love bragging about getting students with less “typical” backgrounds. But then the thought of even the smartest first year law student in the world co-counseling and crossing a key witness in a super high profile murder case is absolutely absurd

Everyone always talks about Atticus Finch as their inspiration for becoming a lawyer, but his advocacy in the trial in To Kill a Mockingbird is fucking horrible lol

I think I’m more sensitive to how consistent the writing is—often stylization can make the very question of suspension of disbelief by giving the insight that it’s just as much someone’s strange art dream as it might be straightforward. So in that case, clearly more metaphorical, allegorical, symbolic and readable films fall into this category, which can make more stilted writing styles that immediately try to establish believability and realization tend to suffer when they don’t live up to a standard of consistency Namely in most genre productions like sci-fi Fantasy, or Horror. This way something like the French animated film and 1973 Cannes special prize winner, [Fantastic Planet](https://www.criterion.com/films/28636-fantastic-planet), Solaris, Arrival, or even movies like Triangle of sadness (which I’ll remind you has like 10 mins of people vomiting) and Freddy got fingered don’t have the suspension of disbelief question occur because you already have to accept they have some specific exaggeration to them. Even EO, a film about a donkey going on an adventure counts. Likewise some Mad Maxes.

Where suspension of disbelief reenters more for me is when movies clarify that they don’t care about your immersion and belief in the setting so much as entertaining in a crunchy content way. like when franchises, adaptations or big-funded projects take themselves for granted or, seeing the bad self-conscious *umm that just happened* recent dialogue.

Like I know I’m punching down, but as mush as I already regretted seeing Dr.strange 2, in theaters, I was so amazingly taken out of the experience by how suprised and angered that the “ice cream song” was kept in the movie as a critical plot point. I know child actors are difficult, but multiple people had to oversee this direct, approve, and decide not to do a retake or cut it entirely.

It really depends.  I love ridiculous action movies but if an otherwise serious movie makes a weird miraculous turn I tend to dislike it.  I dislike it when things work out too cutely, in a world that otherwise seems to be the normal real world.

It depends on the sort of film it is. If the film gives me cues that it's trying to be realistic or would be be better for being realistic, then it might bother me if it isn't living up to that. A good example would be the 2006 film "the lives of others" where authenticity to the time period of the late GDR is crucial to how compelling the narrative is, but in this case it doesn't quite hit the mark.

But I'm not going to care about the realism of a giallo film, becuase it's clearly beside the point. There are films when even internal consistency can be thrown out the window, like for example if it's obviously a work of surrealism or if there is an event that is clearly shown as being miraculous or magical. For me what matters is the expressiveness of the film, and if realism is part of the mode of expression then it hurts if it can't pull it off but if it's not then it doesn't.

In the end though, it's not a matter of suspending disbelief. Suspension of disbelief is always total, realism would be something I see in the film as part of the message. I would have a very hard time not suspending disbelief, as that would amount to suspending my belief in reality (That happens, if your very tired or delirious for some reason, but it tends to go the other way then where reality feels like a movie). I suppose films are like dreams for me, they don't need to make sense. What matters is what meaning or enjoyment is to be had from them.

Thank you for that - a good summery, and yes, that's exactly what I was asking about.

Now I want to see a realistic story about the boring process. One of my all-time favorite movies is 'Margin Call' (2011) which describes a detailed financial process in the most vivid, dramatic light. If you know of a comparable legal drama, please let me know.

I can buy into anything that buys into itself. 100%, full belief, deep dive. But as soon as they break their own rules, or get self referential, or too “clever”, then I’m out, and I’m watching as a critic. It doesn’t happen that often, but there’s so much to watch these days that I can be so much pickier.

>E.g. Total Recall (1990). If you want me to believe the action may be taking place in Quaid's head, don't show me extended scenes with action of which Quaid is completely unaware.

Tbh, it’s a while since I’ve seen Total Recall so I’m not going to throw myself in front of any bullets for it, but I’m not sure about this. I don’t think a story told from one character’s perspective has to be a literal representation of their experience as it happens. Events that a character might not be aware of in the moment can be events they became aware of after the fact or at the moment they enter the scene, and what the audience sees is effectively recounted in the ‘past tense’

In the case of Total Recall, the whole point is to confound either interpretation. Either the events were real, in which case we’re just seeing things as they happened, or they weren’t, in which case what we’re seeing represents information that’s been artificially implanted in Quaid’s head. Again, it’s a while since I saw it, but I don’t think the shifts in POV are necessarily lazy storytelling
Like an 8/10. I like consistency and sound logic. I can suspend my disbelief a bit if movies stick to their own logic and characters make smart decisions. But how often does that happen?
Did you watch The Fall of the House of Usher?  I found the legal bits so dumb I had to shut it off.

Its three things: if the premise and going-ons of the plot are treated seriously BY the characters in the film, if the "rules" of the world of the film are largely internally consistent and - most importantly - if the energy is such that one is swept up in it - than it works for me.
[removed]

It depends on the universe the movie has set itself up as like for example if someone in fairly oddparents survived a car crash with no injuries I'd be fine with that because that show doesn't take itself seriously but if Danny phantom did that I'd roll my eyes as that universe takes itself more seriously than fairly oddparents.

If it's a character focused film, I'm willing to suspend my disbelief more, but it also requires that the characters are well devoloped, otherwise I won't be so kind. A classic example is Vertigo, I really don't give a fuck that it has a ridiculous premise.

>I don't care if a movie is "realistic," but I do want it to make sense. That is, I want it to be consistent with its own premises, however wacky those premises may be.

This is important. I find it infuriating when i watch scifi/fantasy/superheroes etc. and if i say that a decision didn't make sense or something like that, there is always someone responding with "your movie has wozards and space gods and whatever and you complain about it not making sense🤬".

Even if your movie has an unrealistic premise, it will bother me of the internal rules are broken or characters make decisions that don't fit their character.

If i watch a marvel movie and all of a sudden gravity just stops working with no explanation or reaction from anyone, of course it will take me out of the movie.
I'm the same. Stories have their own internal logic, different from the real world. As long as that logic remains consistent, I'm in.
I appreciate when they get stuff right, I don't really care when they don't. I spend most of my life in a state of disbelief so it's nice to suspend it every now and then for a movie.
My cousin vinny is surprisingly accurate though. So accurate in fact that law students are encouraged to watch it because of its realistic depiction of court trials.

I love fantasy and sci fi so I generally don’t really have much issue. However the latest King Kong vs Godzilla movie took the cake for me. Yes I know it’s about an impossibly giant atomic lizard fighting an impossibly giant gorilla but the whole hollow earth stuff just had me like ehhhhh lol. I still enjoyed the movie overall tho

I can forgive nearly anything so long as it's internally consistent, and sensible with regard to that consistency. If dragons and magic are real, totally fine with it. But if a person is show to be able to say, read minds, but then doesn't use that ability when it counts, that ruins the immersion.

There's two takes which are equally important, as you're pointing out. I can accept magic and dragons, superpowers, supernatural elements, whatever, so long as it's internally consistent. That's fine.

But when a movie tries to handle "real" scenarios, I have very little tolerance for nonsense. I can handwave away stuff that's necessary for storytelling purposes (like there always bring the enough ambient light to see what's going on, even in the middle of the night or in a cave, for example) but when movies or shows straight up get things wrong it takes me right out of it. 

I forget which author it was but he was talking about detail in writing, and used the example of lockpicking, and said unless you KNOW what the right details to include are, don't include any, because guaranteed you'll say "latch plate" and someone will write in and say "actually you meant strike plate"

I agree that the witches were real, but we can be shown things that are myths, ideas, imagination, etc. Just because we see the witches on screen doesn't necessarily mean they were real, it could simply be a visual representation of what the family believed or worried might be in the woods. The benchmark for something being real is multiple characters interacting with it independently of each other, and even then some movies play with that idea, Fight Club famously does it, because they switch which character is "real" at any given point. Sometimes the real character is the narrator, sometimes it's Tyler.

I know, but why wait for someone to live in the house? Clearly it could go out to pick that ball in the river, it could go out to flip that car. Why then wait for George C Scott to move into the house to manifest again? Why wait all that time to haunt the girl whose bedroom was covering the well? It looked like it could have done the haunting well before that and communicate who he was? Anyway, that’s nitpicking a bit, I know, still a good film. But since OP asked…
Oh ok. I was not aware of that.

>I agree that the witches were real, but we can be shown things that are myths, ideas, imagination, etc. 

I'm not sure what part of what I said you're disagreeing with. Your examples are exactly the kind of subjectivity I'm talking about and saying The VVitch doesn't use.

It’s been forever since I’ve seen it but I don’t really remember any “law” really being “practiced” in Michael Clayton lol. Michael’s whole role was being like a fixer who helped cover things up for clients (sometimes in an outwardly illegal way), rather than do any kind of “formal” representation of them. 

I have no idea if “big” firms actually do that kind of stuff or to what extent it’s normal, because it would have to all be off the books. But my honest guess is that it’s not really that normal at all, or definitely not in the way the film portrays, because I imagine even the scummiest firm not wanting to be so directly involved in illegal / unethical (in a legal sense) actions like that. And definitely not with someone who they list on their payroll as a lawyer. Like they  may want to retain fancy expensive clients, but most lawyers aren’t exactly in the habit of sticking their necks out so far for clients that it risks them getting in serious legal trouble themselves. Even though lawyers will publicly act like their clients are being wronged or whatever, behind the scenes it tends to be a different story: a lot of managing expectations, a lot of warning them of the risks involved in whatever they’re doing, a lot of convincing them that it may actually be in their best interest to settle or reach a plea deal or whatever. And a lot of hoping and praying that the clients actually fucking listen to the advice that they pay you to give lol
